intro: What Work Was For: a field report from before the timesheet.
outro: What was work for? It was the part of the day that bought the rest of the day.

lines.pre: Ever wonder what work was for? It started with
lines.triplet: The Necessary Motion: you bend, you gather, you repeat.
The First Division: the boy who won't sit still is sent out with the hounds.
The Shared Burden: no one tracks who did how much. The day ends when there is enough.
The First Obligation detaches production from appetite: you bend because you are the bender.
The Bell: the day has owners, and the owners are calling.
The Whistle converts time into currency you spend. The factory's breath commands the herd.
The Long Day: fourteen hours of the sun, all belonging to the mill.
The Hour Saved: the fiercest battle of the century was over the right to go to sleep.

lines.pre: Meanwhile a man with a clipboard invented
lines.triplet: The Stopwatch, breaking any job into terrifyingly efficient micro-motions. He timed every breath.
The Optimised Body, the first manual for treating flesh like gears.
The Pin Factory: no one here knows how to make a pin.
The Division of Labour: no worker sees the whole object.

lines.pre: Where does the rest go? Into
lines.triplet: The Surplus: the factory cannot function if the worker takes home what they make.

lines.pre: Marx had a word for it:
lines.triplet: Alienation. You build the world, but you do not live in it.
The Iron Cage: the Puritan wanted to work in a calling; we are forced to do so.
The Cubicle was invented to give you room? Used to fence you in.
The Knowledge Worker, who cannot be coerced; must be manipulated and persuaded.
The Memo, replacing the factory whistle with ambient dread.
The Meeting, which stops all actual work while simulating productivity.
The Cascade: the project takes six weeks because six weeks were allotted.
The Quarterly: the business shapes itself to what the analyst can see.
The Goodhart Metric: door-to-doctor time improved. The patient died.
The Org Chart, a fiction about how decisions flow.
The Reorg, a periodic ritual where everyone pretends things have changed.
The Performance Review, where the organization meets you and pretends to know you.
The Calibration. The line was drawn before anyone looked at your work.

lines.pre: Graeber counted five kinds of useless job. Meet
lines.triplet: The Box-Ticker: a person writes the report no one will read.
The Duct-Taper, re-entering data the machine lost.
The Taskmaster, creating busywork for the capable.
The Flunky, to make a superior feel important.
The Goon? Because the opponent has one too. An arms race of useless aggression.
The Title and the Promotion: you ask them who they are, and they answer what they do.

lines.pre: Who needs a boss when you have
lines.triplet: The Achievement-Subject? The exploiter is at the same time the exploited.
The Burned: you have no one to blame, because the only one pushing was you.
The Mended Thing answers you in a way the spreadsheet never will.
The Craftsman: cannot survive the modern firm's hatred of slowness and mastery.
The Apprentice: the apprentice no longer apprentices. The apprentice is onboarded.
Quiet Quitting: refuses to give the firm more than it pays for.
Lying Flat: do nothing, achieve nothing, want nothing the system wants you to want.
The Side Project: once a hobby, now a lifeboat.
The Fifteen-Hour Week. We got the productivity. We didn't get the time.
The Always-On: work that does not begin, because it has not ended.
The Notification. Someone needed to clear their queue before logging off.
The Pyjama merges the bed and the desk into a single terrifying location.
The Replacement: your job exists because no one has built a machine to do it yet.
The Forced Holiday: leisure planned around work, ended by work.
The Real Leisure: the activity for which work freed you. We have very little left.
The Day did not have to be filled.
The System: after enough repetition, the other ways became unimaginable.
The Calling. The morning is easier when the job and the calling are the same.

lines.pre: So what was it all for?
lines.triplet: The Rest of the Day: the point of it all.
